pending_items.title: Rohingya genocide case: How The Gambia went to The Hague and won
pending_items.content:
Eighty years after the International Court of Justice (ICJ) first sat in The Hague, I walked into the Peace Palace’s Great Hall of Justice to photograph the judges as they took their seats.

They were about to deliver a landmark judgment in a trailblazing case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar. For the first time, the court would find that a state had committed genocide, the " crime of all crimes " as it has been described.

It had been seven years since The Gambia, a slither of a country of less than three million people in West Africa that is named after the river that dissects it, filed the case.

It argued that Myanmar was trying to destroy the Rohingya, a predominantly Muslim minority that has lived in Rakhine State on the country's western coast for generations.

The case was brought under the 1948 Genocide Convention , the UN’s first human rights treaty, drawn up in the wake of the Holocaust to define genocide under international law and require states to prevent and punish it.

In the past, international criminal tribunals have convicted individuals of genocide, such as in courts created to prosecute atrocities committed during the wars in the former Yugoslavia and in Rwanda in the 1990s.

But this time the question before the ICJ, the UN’s highest court which adjudicates mainly in disputes between states, was whether Myanmar itself, as a state actor, can be held responsible.

In 2017, Myanmar’s military burned Rohingya villages , carried out mass killings and widespread rape, and deliberately killed children, the court found. Soldiers shot civilians as they fled, including people trying to swim to safety.

More than 700,000 fled to neighbouring Bangladesh, which now houses the world’s largest refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar , hosting over one million Rohingya refugees.

Some of the survivors and witnesses were already sobbing as they entered the hall.

Arsalan Suleman, the American lawyer who helped The Gambia bring the case and led its legal team, looked composed and greeted me with a confident smile.

The previous day, the court’s press team had shown journalists the two rooms the judges use before entering the courtroom.

In the Green Room, where they put on their black robes and white lace collars, a namecard stood on the table in front of each chair.

The judges then gather in the Red Room, beneath portraits of former court presidents. The press team also showed us the seating plan, so I knew Navi Pillay, the South African judge last month awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, would be the first judge through the door.

I was struck by how many reporters had turned up. The press room was full, so the court streamed the proceedings in its cafeteria. I had 10 minutes inside the courtroom to photograph the opening.

As we waited for the judges to enter, the room fell silent.

I turned my camera towards the judges’ entrance. Along the wood-panelled hall, four stained-glass windows by the Scottish artist Douglas Strachan depict war in reds and purples and a future at peace in blues and whites.

“La Cour!” the usher called, prompting those inside the courtroom to stand as he opened the door. Above him hung Peace through Justice, Albert Besnard’s painting depicting a goddess of peace standing between two warring parties.

Pillay came through first, followed by the other 14 judges who make up the ICJ's bench, each of them to serve nine-year terms by UN member states.

The Gambia had chosen Pillay, a former UN human rights chief, to sit as an ad hoc judge in the case.

Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for her work promoting peace and international law. Hours after the prize was announced on 9 October, the US announced sanctions against the International Criminal Court, where Pillay was one of the first judges.

Also based in The Hague, the ICC prosecutes individuals for crimes including genocide.

Weeks before the Rohingya judgment, Mike Waltz , the US ambassador to the UN, had accused Pillay of trying to lower the threshold for proving genocide in order to target Americans and their allies, and warned that Washington would be "watching" the proceedings closely. But Pillay appeared defiant as she led the judges into the hall.

At the UN’s International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, the ad hoc court she also previously led, Pillay was one of three judges who convicted former Rwandan mayor Jean-Paul Akayesu in 1998.

It was the first time an international court found an individual guilty of genocide. Pillay led the drafting of the part of the judgment that established that rape and other forms of sexual violence can constitute acts of genocide, also a first under international law.

Most recently, she had chaired the UN’s independent commission of inquiry on occupied Palestine and Israel , which concluded last year that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

On 19 November, with Pillay in the nine-to-six majority, the ICJ ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in northern Rakhine State during its military’s horrific attacks on the group nine years earlier.

After the judgement, Suleman celebrated with Rohingya survivors and his colleagues, a silver garland around his neck. Others wore blue, golden, and silver garlands, in keeping with a Rohingya celebratory custom.

“We are very happy that finally we got a positive verdict, and we’ve got almost all of what we asked the court to deliver,” Dawda Jallow, The Gambia’s justice minister and its representative before the court, told Middle East Eye. “This is unprecedented.”

That evening, at Suleman’s hotel a few minutes’ walk away from the Peace Palace, we spoke for an hour about how this extraordinary and unprecedented case came together - and the long and winding path to justice as circuitous as the Gambia river itself.

Suleman is a Muslim American of Pakistani heritage, born and raised in New Orleans. He studied international security at Georgetown University’s School of Foreign Service, before earning a master’s degree in international peace studies from Trinity College Dublin and then as law degree from Harvard Law School.

Now a partner at the US law firm Foley Hoag, he previously served under President Barack Obama as acting US special envoy to the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) , a group of 57 countries with its headquarters in Saudi Arabia that promotes cooperation among its members and aims to represent the interests of the world's Muslim-majority nations.

The relationships he built there helped him bring the idea for a case to The Gambia.

The case put mainland Africa’s smallest country, a Muslim-majority democracy on the Atlantic coast, at the centre of a landmark ruling on genocide.

The Gambia already has pedigree in the field of international justice. Its capital, Banjul, hosts the secretariat of the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights , and a former Gambian justice minister, Fatou Bensouda , went on to become chief prosecutor of the International Criminal Court.

The Gambia’s involvement in what would become the genocide case against Myanmar began in May 2018, when Bangladesh hosted a meeting of OIC foreign ministers in Dhaka.

The Rohingya crisis was on the agenda, including how to help the hundreds of thousands of refugees by then seeking safety in Bangladesh and hold those responsible for abuses in Myanmar to account.

The Gambia’s foreign minister was unable to attend the Dhaka meeting, Suleman said, so President Adama Barrow sent his justice minister, Abubacarr Tambadou, in his place. As part of the meeting, Bangladesh took delegates to the refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar, where Tambadou met Rohingya survivors.

Justice and accountability were already priorities at home. Gambians had voted out longtime ruler Yahya Jammeh in 2016 to end 22 years of authoritarian rule plagued by human rights abuses.

It had also taken a brief military intervention by Senegal, Nigeria and Ghana through the Ecowas bloc of West African states to force Jammeh to step down.

Barrow’s new government had made truth and reconciliation part of its mandate.

Tambadou had spent almost nine years prosecuting genocide at the UN’s Rwanda tribunal.

“So when he met the victims, he knew what he was seeing,” Suleman explained.

Tambadou worked with OIC officials to set up a committee on accountability, which The Gambia chaired.

Around the same time, Suleman and his colleagues at Foley Hoag were exploring whether a case could be brought under the Genocide Convention. When he raised the idea with former contacts at the OIC, one told him to speak to the Gambians.

Suleman met Tambadou in New York that September, during the UN General Assembly. Some early discussions had focused on international criminal tribunals, which prosecute individuals, Suleman recalled.

The ICJ offered a way to hold Myanmar itself responsible. Tambadou invited him to present the committee with legal options in Banjul, the Gambian capital, the following February.

The committee backed an ICJ case, and the OIC’s foreign ministers and heads of state endorsed it.

pending_items.title: Hormuz oil traffic is down 40 percent: Are Iran’s tanker attacks working?
pending_items.content:
Iran has reiterated that it will use “ all available means ” to confront the United States naval blockade, as it has stepped up attacks on tankers attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz, a global oil chokepoint, signalling potential escalation.

Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday that they would “definitely not tolerate” the naval blockade, and would use “all our tools to confront this US aggression”.

“Iran has the right to use any available tool to defend itself in this regard,” he said.

The naval blockade has largely halted Iranian oil exports. It was first imposed in April, but was lifted following the June memorandum of understanding. The blockade was reinstated weeks later after the agreement collapsed.

As Iran’s economy is increasingly squeezed by the US-led economic sanctions, attacks on tankers have also gone up, affecting the flow of oil through the Strait of Hormuz. The disruption to the flow of oil has triggered a global energy crisis.

Attacks on oil tankers and commercial vessels have continued throughout the war, but more recently, a rising number of tankers have erupted in flames after hitting naval mines purportedly placed by Iran. More than 25 tankers have been hit in the past week alone.

According to reports, tankers have continued to make the dangerous journey through the waterway without seeking Iran’s approval, often travelling in the dark and without navigation transponders to avoid alerting Iranian officials.

However, this clandestine approach has come with its own problems.

On Tuesday morning, Iran’s navy said two oil tankers had hit mines and caught fire in the waterway, according to a statement reported by Iran’s Tasnim news agency.

According to the statement, the tankers entered a restricted zone east of the strait after turning off their navigation and identification systems.

The statement reiterated that the strait would not be opened until Iran’s objectives and demands were met, including halting hostilities, lifting the blockade and waiving sanctions, adding that “owners of oil tankers are required to coordinate with the armed forces to ensure safe passage through this strategic strait.”

At the same time, the commander of the Iranian army, Amir Hatami, called for tightening the closure of the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, stressing that Tehran needed to make conditions more difficult.

“We must tighten our control over the Strait of Hormuz, our management of it must be stronger, and conditions must become more difficult for the enemy,” Iranian television quoted Hatami as saying, during a speech to senior army commanders at the Command and Staff University.

The head of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC) navy, Ali Ozmaei, also warned vessels passing through the Strait of Hormuz against using unapproved shipping routes.

“The Strait of Hormuz is not a place to test unauthorised routes and ignore maritime warnings,” Ozmaei said, according to the ISNA news agency.

Despite the attacks, oil prices have fallen, with Brent crude futures at $88.35 per barrel as supplies recover . At one point, oil prices went past $120 per barrel.

So far, according to the AIS ship-tracking platform, in the past 24 hours, 28 ships have crossed the strait: 12 into the Gulf and 16 out of it, carrying an estimated 4.18 million barrels of oil.

However, because it only collects data from vessels with transponders on, loopholes – including the no-signal bypass routes – mean it is not an accurate count of how many ships are crossing the strait.

Still, it is a huge drop from pre-war numbers, during which 125 to 140 ships used to pass through daily.

In the past week, Iran has also carried out attacks on US bases in the Gulf, targeting radars.

On Sunday, US President Donald Trump said in a post on Truth Social that Iran had launched “more drones and missiles in the last week than at any time for over a year”, adding that they had all been downed and had caused no damage.

Meanwhile, last week, US Central Command ( CENTCOM ) said in an advisory that ships receiving cargo from vessels loaded at Iranian ports or along the country’s coastline could be considered to be “evading the blockade”, which had allowed some Iranian petroleum products to reach international markets.

But Iran has repeatedly warned against US efforts to hamper its trade.

According to data from Marine Traffic, a ship-tracking platform, the number of vessels crossing between November 1 and 23 has dropped as the month goes on.

In the first week of November, between the 1st and 7th, 226 vessels entered or exited the Gulf. In the last week of the month, from the 17th to the 23rd, only 125 vessels crossed the waterway. That’s a drop of more than 40 percent.

Throughout the month, the highest day with 29 vessels exiting took place on November 1, and the highest day entering the Gulf was November 7.

In contrast, the lowest day for exiting the Gulf was on Sunday, when only one vessel left the waterway; on the same day, only two vessels entered the waterway, the lowest figure for the month.

pending_items.title: Israel kills senior Hamas security official in airstrike on Gaza
pending_items.content:
CAIRO, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Israel killed a senior Hamas security official in an airstrike on Gaza on Tuesday which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said showed there was no escape from his country's "long reach."

Naeem Abu Nahel, the director of Hamas' internal security apparatus in Gaza, was one of at least seven Palestinians killed in the Gaza Strip, including two police officers, Palestinian medics and police said.

The interior ministry in Gaza, led by the Palestinian militant group Hamas, said Israel had "assassinated" Abu Nahel for his role in fighting collaborators and Israeli-backed armed militias seeking to topple the group in the tiny enclave.

Netanyahu commended the Israeli military for killing Abu Nahel, whom he mentioned by name, less than two months after Israeli forces captured his predecessor in an undercover raid into Gaza.

"No terrorist will manage to escape the long reach of the State of Israel," a statement issued by Netanyahu's office said.

A key mission of Abu Nahel's internal security service is to counter Palestinians suspected of collaboration with Israel's secret service and gather information about its plans.

The Israeli military and the Shin Bet domestic security service said in a joint statement earlier on Tuesday that they had struck a senior Hamas militant, without identifying him, adding that further details would be provided later.

Netanyahu, who built his reputation as a security hawk, is serving as caretaker prime minister after his right-wing bloc lost its parliamentary majority in an election last month.

President Isaac Herzog has tasked Netanyahu's centre-right rival Gadi Eisenkot with forming a government but he also lacks a majority and Netanyahu is battling to stay in power.

Palestinian medics said three people were also killed in an Israeli airstrike at a police post in Khan Younis in southern Gaza. The interior ministry in Gaza said two of them were police officers.

Five other people were wounded in the attack, medics added.

Another Israeli airstrike near the Netzarim corridor further north killed another three people, taking Tuesday's death toll to at least seven.

The Israeli military told Reuters it had struck militants in both areas.

An October ⁠2025 US-backed ceasefire halted major fighting in the shattered territory, but has not stopped Israeli attacks on Gaza or secured Hamas' disarmament.

Israel, which accuses Hamas of trying to regroup and rearm, has stepped up its attacks in Gaza in recent months. Hamas denies the Israeli allegations, saying it is committed to the ceasefire agreement and accusing Israel of trying to derail it.

At least 1,600 Palestinians and five ​Israeli soldiers have been killed since then, according to respective Palestinian and Israeli tallies.

Israeli ​troops now ⁠control around two-thirds of Gaza, up from more than half at the time of the ceasefire, with Hamas controlling a sliver of territory along Gaza's coast.

Israel's assault on Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians since 2023, caused a ⁠hunger ​crisis, internally displaced Gaza's entire population and led to assessments of genocide ​from scholars and a United Nations inquiry.

Israel has said its actions were in self-defence after Hamas-led militants killed 1,200 people and took more than ​250 hostages in an attack on Israel in October 2023.

(Reporting by Nidal al-Mughrabi. Additional reporting by Eman Abouhassira; Editing by Christopher Cushing, Andrew Heavens and Timothy Heritage)

pending_items.title: Ahmad Tibi ‘most threatened’ MP in Israel amid rising anti-Palestinian incitement
pending_items.content:
Palestinian lawmaker and Israeli citizen Ahmad Tibi is the most "threatened" member of Israel's parliament, according to the Knesset's security chief.

Israel Hayom reported on Monday that Tibi, a member of the Palestinian-led Joint List alliance, had been told to "take care of himself and be careful" by Yuval Chen, commander of the Knesset Guard, the security unit responsible for protecting Israel's parliament.

Chen reportedly told Tibi that he was “the most threatened member of the Knesset”.

Sources in the Joint List accused the Knesset Guard of failing to provide adequate protection for Palestinian lawmakers inside the Knesset.

"Where are the Knesset Guard officers when they are needed? Why aren't they stationed permanently at the door of the Joint List during parliamentary group meetings?" they told the Israeli newspaper.

The warning to Tibi follows an incident on Monday in which Israeli comedian and right-wing figure Guy Hochman put his arms around the lawmaker while attempting to film a video.

Tibi pushed Hochman away after the comedian entered his personal space, prompting accusations that the Palestinian MP had assaulted him.

Hochman filed a complaint against Tibi with the Knesset Guard, alleging that the lawmaker had assaulted him. Ma'ariv also reported that a complaint against Tibi had been submitted to Israel's attorney general, Gali Baharav-Miara.

Tibi, however, said he felt threatened when Hochman invaded his personal space on Knesset premises and that he had acted in self-defence.

"Hochman is a bad actor. He suddenly shoved a phone in my face, I pushed the phone away, and since then I've been told he went into intensive care," Tibi told Ma'ariv.

Tibi said he had also filed a complaint against Hochman with the Knesset Guard, saying he had "felt threatened".

In a letter to the security unit, Tibi said Hochman had "approached me from behind, grabbed me without my consent, and shoved a phone to my face in an invasive and threatening manner".

"The incident is especially serious against the backdrop of the threats, incitement, and smears directed at me since the elections," the letter said.

It referred to the growing incitement against Tibi by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies since the Joint List and Ra'am won a historic 19 seats in the Knesset in last month's elections.

Tibi also accused the Knesset Guard of discriminating against Palestinian lawmakers.

"It is highly doubtful that an Arab man who behaved this way towards a Jewish minister would have received similar treatment, without the immediate intervention of the guards, who would have slammed him to the ground," he said.

"The security and dignity of Arab Knesset Members are not fair game," Tibi added, demanding an investigation into the incident.

Meanwhile, far-right Israeli politicians used the confrontation to launch fresh attacks against the Palestinian lawmaker.

Outgoing Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich urged Jewish opposition parties, led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, not to form a government dependent on votes from the Joint List and Ra'am.

"This is what happens when they feel like the masters of the land; parliamentary violence turns into physical violence," Smotrich said , accusing Tibi of assaulting Hochman.

"The police must immediately open a criminal investigation against Ahmad Tibi," the settler leader added on X.

Two MPs from the party of outgoing National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir, Otzma Yehudit, also attacked Tibi.

On Monday, Tally Gotliv stormed a Joint List parliamentary group meeting, while Hanamel Dorfman wrote on X: "The doctor of terror is also a doctor of violence."

Tibi, who was elected last week as one of the Knesset's deputy speakers, has become a prominent target of the far-right incitement campaign against Palestinians in Israel since the elections.

He is not the only Palestinian to face such hostility.

Last week, a mosque in the village of Ed-Dahi was set on fire in a suspected arson attack linked to an Israeli mob.

pending_items.content:
Yemen’s Houthi-run Economy Ministry says Saudi attacks and the blockade have inflicted more than $1.13 trillion in cumulative economic losses since the war began began in March 2015.

Acting Economy Minister Sam al-Bashiri said preliminary estimates put direct damage during the latest escalation, from 13 July to 23 November, at more than $881.5 million, Saba reports.

He said Saudi strikes destroyed 22 factories and partially damaged three others, causing industrial losses exceeding $376 million.

The ministry put commercial losses above $85 million and investment-sector losses above $20 million.

Transport and Public Works Minister Mohammed Quhaim reported more than $350 million in damage to infrastructure and other sectors during the same period.

Quhaim said attacks on airports, ports, roads and bridges had disrupted supplies and increased shipping, insurance and storage costs, placing further financial pressure on Yemenis.

The announcement provided no detailed methodology for the cumulative trillion-dollar estimate.
